etymologies.etymologyHTML: From low +‎ -er (comparative suffix).

definitions.definition: comparative form of low: more low
Bottom; more towards the bottom than the middle of an object.
Situated on lower ground, nearer a coast, or more southerly.
(geology, of strata or geological time periods) Older.
comparative form of low: more low
(transitive) To let descend by its own weight, as something suspended; to let down

quote.citation: 1833 (first publication), Alfred Tennyson, A Dream of Fair Women
quote.text: Lower'd softly with a threefold cord of loveDown to a silent grave.

quote.citation: 1960 September, “Talking of Trains: New level-crossing signs”, in Trains Illustrated, page 519:
quote.text: At level crossings where there are to be half-barriers, train-operated through track-circuiting, the barriers will be timed to lower fully about five seconds before the fastest train can reach the crossing.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reduce the degree, intensity, strength, etc., of
(reflexive) To humble oneself; to do something one considers to be beneath one's dignity.
(transitive) To reduce (something) in value, amount, etc.
(intransitive) To fall; to sink; to grow less; to diminish; to decrease
(intransitive) To decrease in value, amount, etc.
(computing, transitive) To reduce operations to single machine instructions, as part of compilation of a program.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: lower (third-person singular simple present lowers, present participle lowering, simple past and past participle lowered)

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), [William Shakespeare], The Tragedy of King Richard the Third. […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  Valentine Sims [and Peter Short] for Andrew Wise, […], published 1597, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: Now is the winter of our diſcontent, / Made glorious ſummer by this ſonne of Yorke: / And all the cloudes that lowrd vpon our houſe, / In the deepe boſome of the Ocean buried.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Homer’s Ilias”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, book I, page 215:
quote.text: [...] Juno took her place: / But ſullen Diſcontent ſat lowring on her Face.

quote.citation: 1846, R[obert] S[tephen] Hawker, “The Wreck”, in Echoes from Old Cornwall, London: Joseph Masters, […], →OCLC, stanza X, page 76:
quote.text: And still when loudliest howls the storm, / And darkliest lowers his native sky, / The king's fierce soul is in that form, / The warrior's spirit threatens nigh!
